abstract: Many nocturnal moths have evolved tympanal hearing to detect echolocating bats, and evade them by turning away, diving and flying erratically. These responses are well studied separately, but how free-flying moths combine them in a single escape, and which aerodynamic forces drive them, remains poorly understood. We analysed escape responses of tomato looper moths (Chrysodeixis chalcites) exposed to a bat-like ultrasound buzz (40 kHz) in a greenhouse. We reconstructed 447 flight trajectories from 11 ultrasound nights and 22 no-sound control nights. Before the stimulus, moths flew about 0.3 m s-1 faster on ultrasound nights, suggesting a sustained response to predation risk. Within 0.1-0.2 s of sound onset, moths dived at about 13° below the horizontal, irrespective of sound direction. They increased flight speed by 0.6 m s-1 and aerodynamic force by 0.7 times their body weight. A passive drop would have reduced the aerodynamic force, so the escape dives were powered. Escape directions were highly variable (circular standard deviation 74°), but on average pointed almost directly away from the sound (average offset 2°). This required a directional response to the sound. Moths with the source in front turned about 60° more than controls, and those with the source behind them about 25° more. Consequently, 80% ended with the source behind them (controls: 58%). Threatened moths thus fly faster before and during the escape, and steer powered dives away from the threat, yet unpredictably. Combining directional bias with variability may be a general escape strategy against fast, manoeuvrable predators.
